rv.q: This multifaceted and personal homage to – and collaboration with – composer Philip Glass is a transcendent tapestry suffused with joy and wonder.
Director, writer and actor Phelim McDermott’s musing on creativity and his relationship with composer Philip Glass and his music strikes me as quite beautiful, but some will find it exasperating.
Tao of Glass is many things; delightfully funny, visually impressive, challengingly erudite and exquisitely beautiful.
Tao of Glass overflows with generosity and spirituality.
Dense, profound, a lecture with stage play and comedy to help it go down, Tao of Glass is a delight, but you must stay alert.
Fortunately, for the most part, it also happens to be bloody marvellous.
Thoughtful, visually striking and emotionally resonant, Tao of Glass invites audiences to slow down, listen and reflect.
It’s fantastical and disarming in a way that normally seems out of reach for adult theatre.
Otherwise, the art of storytelling blossoms in this curious and fascinating show.
And McDermott himself is totally enthralling.
Tao of Glass is a show like no other and one that deserves to be seen to be believed.
It feels close to miraculous that a piece this experimental, this gentle and this patient can exist on a West End stage.
But, at nearly three hours, it feels somewhat indulgent, and the musical elements are subsumed by the storytelling.

cn.t: McDermott's deeply personal homage to Philip Glass divides critics but mostly enchants with its imaginative blend of puppetry, music, and memoir. Some find it transcendent and joyful; others consider it pretentious or uneven across its two acts.
